bull.t: IET order momentum and backlog visibility
bull.b: Record IET bookings, a 2.2x book-to-bill ratio, and record RPO create substantial multi-year revenue visibility. This backlog supports planning and capacity utilization, reduces reliance on immediate project wins, and strengthens Baker Hughes’ position in LNG, power, and gas infrastructure markets.

Healthy operating and free cash flow provide internally generated funding for investment, debt reduction, and shareholder returns. Combined with improved margins, this indicates meaningful earnings power and gives Baker Hughes greater resilience while it expands its industrial and energy technology portfolio.

Chart broadens Baker Hughes beyond traditional oilfield exposure toward thermal management, industrial infrastructure, and aftermarket activities. The identified cost and commercial synergies provide a concrete path to wider product coverage, more recurring revenue, and potentially stronger consolidated margins over time.

bear.b: The sharp increase in debt-to-equity raises balance-sheet risk and reduces flexibility in a cyclical industry. Higher leverage can constrain future investment and capital allocation, while increasing sensitivity to weaker energy activity; management’s planned deleveraging therefore remains important to the fundamental outlook.

A sharply negative TTM revenue-growth reading raises questions about the consistency of top-line expansion, even though profitability has improved. Volatile revenue can make utilization, earnings planning, and cash generation less predictable, limiting the durability of recent margin gains across future industry cycles.

Strong order intake does not translate into near-term revenue when long GTE cycles and aero-derivative supply-chain timing defer conversion beyond 2027. This creates a gap between bookings and reported growth, leaving near-term results more dependent on execution of the existing business.
